content.intro: Learn production settings and environment through a compact visual, an inspectable Django example, and a practical verification task.
content.why_it_matters: Production Settings and Environment matters because a Django project has to behave predictably across requests, database state, configuration, and deployments. Understanding this piece makes the surrounding application easier to test, maintain, and secure.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: This lesson examines production settings and environment as part of deployment and production operations. The objective is to understand the behavior, connect it to the listed subtopics, and verify it with a small example rather than relying on memorized syntax.

content_blocks.title: What to cover
content_blocks.text: The source syllabus for this lesson names: Secure environment variables; DEBUG = False; ALLOWED_HOSTS; Database configuration; Separating public configuration from secrets. Keep these distinct concepts together: know what each item does, when it applies, and what assumption must be verified in your project.

items.title: Secure environment variables
items.text: Environment variables separate deploy-time configuration from source control. Validate required settings at startup and never put real secret values in examples, frontend code, logs, or committed `.env` files.

items.title: DEBUG = False
items.text: Treat DEBUG = False as a reproducible diagnostic: capture the exact input and observed result, isolate one hypothesis, and add a regression test once the cause is fixed. Avoid exposing internal stack traces or secrets to public users.

items.title: ALLOWED_HOSTS
items.text: For ALLOWED_HOSTS, identify the Django component responsible, the inputs and outputs it owns, and the boundary conditions that matter. Use the accompanying example as a starting point, verify it with the official versioned documentation, and record one test demonstrating expected behavior.

items.title: Database configuration
items.text: Configuration for Database configuration should be explicit, environment-aware, and validated before serving requests. Record defaults and deploy-specific values, keep secrets outside committed content, and test the setting that changes behavior.

items.title: Separating public configuration from secrets
items.text: Secrets belong in protected runtime configuration or a secret manager with least-privilege access and rotation plans. Never commit, log, return or embed production credentials in client code.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: First identify the input and the responsible Django component. Next trace how the example moves through “Production Settings and Environment” and the related concept “Secure environment variables”. Predict the result before running or inspecting it. Finally compare the observed behavior with the expected result and the cited official documentation.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Change one input or configuration choice related to Secure environment variables. Write down the expected outcome, test one normal case and one invalid or boundary case, then record what changed. Do not add real credentials or sensitive production data.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Common pitfalls include skipping a required configuration/import, copying a fragment without its model or URL context, trusting client input, or treating a development-only behavior as production-ready. Check the earliest failing assumption, consult the version-specific docs, and add a regression test for the failure you found.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to describe production settings and environment, explain the listed topics, inspect the example, and choose an appropriate verification step. Keep the scope and version caveat visible when sharing your solution.
